LiteResearcher: A Scalable Agentic RL Training Framework for Deep Research Agent

Wanli Li1,2,∗, Bince Qu1,2,∗, Bo Pan1, Jianyu Zhang1, Zheng Liu3,†, Pan Zhang2
Wei Chen1, Bo Zhang1,2,† 1 Zhejiang University  2 Simplex AI  3 The Hong Kong Polytechnic University {wanli_li@zju.edu.cn, tonyzhang@simplexai.com} https://github.com/simplex-ai-inc/LiteResearcher  https://huggingface.co/simplex-ai-inc/LiteResearcher-4B
Abstract

Reinforcement Learning (RL) has emerged as a powerful training paradigm for LLM-based agents. However, scaling agentic RL for deep research remains constrained by two coupled challenges: hand-crafted synthetic data fails to elicit genuine real-world search capabilities, and real-world search dependency during RL training introduces instability and prohibitive cost, which limits the scalability of Agentic RL. LiteResearcher is a training framework that makes Agentic RL scalable: by constructing a lite virtual world that mirrors real-world search dynamics, we enable a continuously improving training recipe that empowers a tiny search agent to outperform large-scale open-source and commercial models (e.g., Tongyi DeepResearch and Claude-4.5 Sonnet). Specifically, on common benchmarks such as GAIA and Xbench, our LiteResearcher-4B achieves open-source state-of-the-art results of 71.3% and 78.0% respectively, demonstrating that scalable RL training is a key enabler for Deep Research Agents.

1 Introduction

Recent advances in reinforcement learning (RL) on reasoning models (Liu et al., 2025b; Guo et al., 2025; Team et al., 2025a) have demonstrated that continuously scaling model capabilities is achievable within stable training environments and with data of appropriate difficulty. However, when transitioning to agentic RL, where reasoning must be integrated with tool use, prior efforts have struggled to achieve similar sustained improvements. We identify the primary bottleneck as the inherent noise and instability of the real-world environment. In the domain of Coding Agents (Wei et al., 2025b; Jain et al., 2025), this challenge has been effectively addressed through the use of isolated sandboxes configured to simulate production environments while filtering out infrastructure-level noise, thereby enabling scalable training.

However, existing works in the domain of Deep Research have yet to realize such scalable RL training. Online RL frameworks (Zheng et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025d) interact directly with the live internet, introducing significant training variance and prohibitive costs that limit continuous capability growth. Local retrieval-based systems (Jin et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025c; Sun et al., 2025) are typically confined to a narrow corpus, making it impossible to replicate the complex search dynamics of the diverse internet. Meanwhile, current real-web graph-based data synthesis methods (Jin et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025a; Gao et al., 2025) rely on over-engineered reasoning structures, focusing on handcrafted logic while ignoring the diversity of atomic search techniques required for deep research, such as cross-verification and enumeration.

We argue that scaling agentic RL for Deep Research requires a virtual world that mirrors the structure of the live internet but is isolated in execution: the twin architecture ensures that policies optimized in the virtual environment can generalize to the open web, while isolation shields the training process from the high variance and stochasticity of environmental noise.

In this paper, we present LiteResearcher, an Agentic RL training framework designed to construct a virtual world that mirrors real-world web architecture. We follow these steps to realize the scaling potential of agentic RL: (1) Synthesize real search data; (2) Simulate search environment; (3) Achieve sustained improvements through curriculum RL.

The foundation of this virtual world is generating realistic training tasks. To capture the diversity of information seeking in real-world user queries, we prioritize the scale of information sources in our virtual world. We find that by scaling up information sources, even a simple-but-effective data synthesis can yield a realistic distribution of training tasks.

Crucially, handling these synthetic tasks requires a corresponding execution environment. We simulate a realistic search environment by enriching our corpus with these tasks. For every synthetic task, we perform a targeted expansion of the local webpage corpus by searching and fetching related real-world webpages, which then construct the local search and browse tool. This ensures that for any given training task, the local search and browse tools provide search dynamics analogous to the open web, allowing the agent to obtain real-web atom capabilities in a controlled environment.

Even with synthetic tasks and tools, training can still saturate if the model gets trapped at a certain difficulty threshold, correctly solving easy tasks while completely failing complex ones. We apply a difficulty-aware curriculum RL which progressively enhances both task difficulty and context length across training stages. At each stage, we only keep the synthetic tasks that the current model can partially solve, discarding both trivially easy and impossibly hard instances, thereby providing consistent training signal for improvement.

Our tiny search agent LiteResearcher-4B achieves 71.3% on GAIA (Mialon et al., 2023) and 78.0% on Xbench (Chen et al., 2025), surpassing open-source agents up to 8×8\times larger such as Tongyi DeepResearch 30B (70.9%/75.0%) and WebSailor 30B (53.2%/53.3%), while matching or exceeding proprietary systems including Claude-4.5-Sonnet (71.2%/66.0%) and GLM-4.6 (71.9%/70.0%). These results demonstrate that scalable RL can yield a powerful on-device deep research agent.

2 Related Work

Reinforcement Learning for Reasoning

The pursuit of advanced reasoning in LLMs initially relied on inference-time heuristics such as Chain-of-Thought prompting (Wei et al., 2022) and Tree of Thoughts (Yao et al., 2023). A paradigm shift occurred with the demonstration that RL can internalize reasoning capabilities directly into model weights. DeepSeek-R1 (Guo et al., 2025) showed that RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is sufficient to unlock emergent reasoning behaviors such as self-verification and backtracking, and subsequent work has rapidly advanced optimization (Yu et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025b), reward design (Cui et al., 2025), and scaling (Hu et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025), establishing RLVR as a general-purpose post-training paradigm. However, all these methods operate as closed-world reasoners: they rely solely on parametric knowledge and lack the ability to interact with external dynamic environments—a critical limitation for tasks requiring real-time information retrieval.

Agentic Deep Research Models

Recent research has pivoted towards Agentic Deep Research, where agents interact with external search environments through iterative query formulation and page navigation. This line of work can be grouped by environment design. Online real-world RL systems (Zheng et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025d; Li et al., 2025a) train directly on the live web, offering realistic interactions but incurring high cost and non-deterministic reward signals. Local retrieval-based systems (Jin et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025c; Gao et al., 2025) construct environments from Wikipedia or similar corpora, providing fast, deterministic interactions but remaining confined to narrow, homogeneous domains. Simulated systems such as ZeroSearch (Sun et al., 2025) replace search engines by training an LLM to mimic search engine outputs, but sacrifice page-level fidelity. Recent lightweight explorations such as AgentCPM-Explore (Chen et al., 2026) further show the capability of small deep-research agents, but still fail to realize scalable RL training. In contrast, our framework builds a local environment with real-world data and a search engine, enabling scalable RL training.

3 Preliminaries: Agentic Framework

We model deep research as a sequential decision-making process under the ReAct framework (Yao et al., 2022). Given an initial user query qq, the agent interacts with the environment over multiple steps by alternately generating reasoning thoughts, executing actions, and receiving observations. The history up to step tt is denoted by

ℋt=(q,τ1,a1,o1,…,τt,at,ot),\mathcal{H}_{t}=(q,\tau_{1},a_{1},o_{1},\dots,\tau_{t},a_{t},o_{t}),

where τi\tau_{i}, aia_{i}, and oio_{i} denote the thought, action, and environmental observation at step ii, respectively. At each step, the agent first generates a reasoning thought τt\tau_{t} conditioned on the preceding history, and then selects an executable action ata_{t} conditioned on both ℋt−1\mathcal{H}_{t-1} and τt\tau_{t}:

τt∼πθ(⋅∣ℋt−1),at∼πθ(⋅∣ℋt−1,τt).\tau_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\mathcal{H}_{t-1}),\qquad a_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\mathcal{H}_{t-1},\tau_{t}).

Action Space. The action space 𝒜\mathcal{A} consists of two primitive actions:

  • •

    Search(q′)(q^{\prime}): submits a natural-language query q′q^{\prime} to the search engine and returns a ranked list of retrieved snippets and URLs.

  • •

    Browse(u,q′)(u,q^{\prime}): visits a selected URL uu and returns a query-conditioned summary of the page content.

After collecting sufficient information, the agent terminates environment interaction and generates a final response to the original user query qq.

4 Methods: Towards Scalable Training

To explore the scaling potential of Agentic Deep Research, we aim to establish a scalable training framework as a mandatory first step. Current paradigms that rely on high-latency, unstable online interactions fundamentally bottleneck this process. In this section, we present our LiteResearcher framework, which decouples agent evolution from the open web while ensuring generalization to real-world web dynamics. As illustrated in Figure 2, the ecosystem is built upon three core pillars:

(1) Co-construct Training Data and Corpus Pipeline: To achieve diversity in the data distribution and scalability in data quantity, we propose a unified framework that co-evolves the training data and the local corpus.

(2) Stable Local Tool Environment: Leveraging the enriched webpage corpus, we construct a Local Search Engine and Local Browse Tool that mirror the behavior of real-world search dynamics within the synthesized data.

(3) Difficulty-Aware Curriculum Learning: To continuously expand the model’s capability boundaries, we leverage our unlimited synthetic data pool to implement a multi-stage curriculum that serves the model with data of appropriate difficulty, thereby ensuring sustainable performance improvements.

4.1 Co-construct Training Data and Corpus Pipeline

We identify that complex real-world deep research trajectories are fundamentally composed of five atomic search capabilities:

  • •

    Direct Information: Directly finding a specific piece of information via search.

  • •

    Aggregation: Locating a target answer based on multiple identifying attributes.

  • •

    Enumeration: Listing and counting all entities that satisfy specific constraints.

  • •

    Cross-verification: Validating and triangulating claims across independent sources.

  • •

    Statistics: Performing comprehensive calculations and extracting numerical metrics.

To construct a dataset with both capability diversity and scalability, rather than relying on complex, handcrafted generation logic, we first scale up the underlying information sources to comprehensively cover the diverse search patterns of the real world. Subsequently, we filter this vast information pool into solvable, high-quality tasks. Specifically:

QA generation from Seed Corpus

The data construction process begins with a high-quality Seed Corpus including Wikipedia and BBC News articles. We then prompt an LLM with the template in Appendix A.1 to process this raw content and extract structured question-answer (QA) pairs that target key factual entities within the content. These initial QA pairs serve as the foundational “seed tasks” that trigger the subsequent iterative expansion of the local environment.

Information Source Masking

To prevent the agent from relying on trivial shortcuts, we implement a source masking mechanism. After a QA pair is generated, we deliberately delete its original information source from the local corpus. This forces the agent to navigate the expanded corpus to discover alternative, non-trivial search pathways, naturally eliciting the complex atomic search capabilities detailed in Table 1.

Strict Quality and Difficulty Filtering

To guarantee the quality and solvability of the dataset, the candidate QA pairs undergo a rigorous LLM-based evaluation guided by a 7-point rubric (Appendix A.2). As detailed in Appendix A.2, this rubric contains dimensions such as independence, ambiguity, answer verifiability, etc. A data point is retained only if it strictly satisfies all seven criteria. Furthermore, prior to each training session, we apply an additional difficulty filter to ensure the tasks are appropriately calibrated to the agent’s current capability (see Section 4.3). This final distillation process provides a diverse and realistic data distribution for subsequent training.

Continuously Expanding Corpus

For each filtered QA pair, we utilize a search engine to fetch related webpages from the live internet. These newly retrieved pages are continuously appended to the Enriched Corpus. This iterative expansion creates a corpus covering the vast and diverse information distribution of the real world.

4.2 Stable Local Tool Environment

Leveraging the enriched corpus from Section 4.1 (∼\sim32M pages, 1M+ domains), we build a fully local tool environment that replaces online interaction during RL training. Unlike standard RAG pipelines that split each page into many chunks, we adopt page-level indexing: each webpage is represented by a single vector (title + summary). This keeps the index small enough to serve hundreds of concurrent rollouts at low latency, which would be infeasible with a chunk-level index that is ∼\sim10×\times larger. During training, the system sustains hundreds of concurrent tool requests, accumulating to 73.2M calls over the full RL run (Section 5). The corpus is served through two purpose-built services (infrastructure details in Appendix D):

  • •

    Local Search Engine: We adopt BGE-M3 (Chen et al., 2024) for hybrid retrieval, which produces both dense and learned sparse embeddings in a single forward pass. The two signals are fused at query time through the built-in hybrid search of Milvus (Wang et al., 2021). All embeddings are stored on disk and accessed via DiskANN (Jayaram Subramanya et al., 2019) with mmap, achieving ∼\sim0.15 s/query (∼\sim10×\times faster than online search engine).

  • •

    Local Browse Tool: Full webpage content is stored as Markdown in PostgreSQL, keyed by URL and tuned for 1,000 concurrent connections; pages are returned directly upon request at ∼\sim0.17 s/page (∼\sim46×\times faster than Jina Reader).

4.3 Difficulty-Aware Curriculum Learning

A fundamental challenge in Agentic RL is training saturation, where the reward curve converges because the model becomes trapped at a difficulty threshold, correctly solving easy tasks while completely failing complex ones, resulting in no meaningful learning gradient.

Difficulty-Aware Data Filtering

To address training saturation, before each RL stage, we evaluate the difficulty of training queries. For each query, we generate K=8K=8 rollouts (pass@8) and strictly retain only those where the number of correct responses cc satisfies 1≤c≤71\leq c\leq 7. Queries with c=8c=8 are discarded as trivial (yielding zero useful gradient), while those with c=0c=0 are deemed impossible or excessively noisy.

On-Policy GRPO Curriculum Learning

We employ the Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024) framework. Given a query qq and sampled outputs {o1,…,oK}\{o_{1},\dots,o_{K}\}, the advantage AiA_{i} is computed by normalizing the reward of oio_{i} against the group mean and standard deviation. Stripped of KL and entropy terms, our objective function is defined strictly as the clipped surrogate loss:

𝒥G​R​P​O​(θ)=𝔼q∼P⁡(Q),{oi}i=1K∼πθo​l​d​[1K​∑i=1Kmin⁡(ri​(θ)​Ai,clip​(ri​(θ),1−ϵl​o​w,1+ϵh​i​g​h)​Ai)]\mathcal{J}_{GRPO}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{q\sim P(Q),\{o_{i}\}_{i=1}^{K}\sim\pi_{\theta_{old}}}\left[\frac{1}{K}\sum_{i=1}^{K}\min\left(r_{i}(\theta)A_{i},\text{clip}\left(r_{i}(\theta),1-\epsilon_{low},1+\epsilon_{high}\right)A_{i}\right)\right]

where ri​(θ)=πθ​(oi|q)πθr​o​l​l​o​u​t​(oi|q)r_{i}(\theta)=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(o_{i}|q)}{\pi_{\theta_{rollout}}(o_{i}|q)} is the probability ratio of training engine and rollout engine. While standard implementations perform multiple mini-batch updates over a replay buffer, we enforce a strictly on-policy update. We present a detailed ablation study regarding this completely on-policy formulation in Section 5.

5 Experiments

5.1 Experimental Setup

We evaluate LiteResearcher-4B on a suite of complex reasoning and agentic search benchmarks, including GAIA (Mialon et al., 2023), BrowseComp (Wei et al., 2025a), HLE (Phan et al., 2025), Frames (Krishna et al., 2025), WebWalker (Wu et al., 2025b), Seal-0 (Pham et al., 2026), and Xbench-DeepSearch-2505 (Chen et al., 2025). For BrowseComp, we randomly sampled 400 examples for evaluation. Evaluation is conducted with online APIs (Serper for search and Jina for browsing), following the same tool setup as prior work (Team et al., 2025c). We compare against leading closed-source foundation models, representative open-source deep-research agents, and AgentCPM-Explore (Chen et al., 2026) as a concurrent lightweight baseline.

All experiments are initialized from Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 (Yang et al., 2025). We first perform a cold-start SFT stage to teach the model basic tool-use capabilities such as query formulation, search invocation, and page browsing (details in Appendix B). The RL stage generates rollouts entirely within our local environment, with a global batch size of 128 (on-policy update), generating 8 rollouts per query. The learning rate is fixed at 1×10−61\times 10^{-6}. The maximum response length is initialized at 32K tokens in the first stage and expanded by 16K tokens in each subsequent stage. Our loss function uses neither a KL divergence penalty nor an entropy regularization term.

5.2 Main Results

Table 2 summarizes the performance of LiteResearcher (4B) across eight benchmarks spanning general-purpose agentic search, multi-hop reasoning, and cross-lingual deep research. From the results, we make the following key observations.

A 4B model trained locally approaches commercial-level performance. LiteResearcher achieves 71.3% on GAIA-Text, matching Claude-4.5-Sonnet (71.2%) and surpassing Tongyi DeepResearch 30B (70.9%) and other open-source models with 8–32B parameters. On Frames, it scores 83.1%, outperforming Claude-4-Sonnet (80.7%) and DeepSeek-V3.2 (80.2%). On Xbench-DS, a comprehensive bilingual benchmark, LiteResearcher reaches 78.0%, the highest among all open-source models and surpassing OpenAI-GPT-5-high (77.8%). These results suggest that the data–environment bottleneck is at least as important as model scale for strong agentic search performance.

Local training matches or exceeds online training. AgentCPM-Explore-4B (Chen et al., 2026), a concurrent 4B model trained on the live internet, is outperformed by LiteResearcher on all 8 benchmarks (e.g., GAIA 71.3% vs. 63.9%, Xbench 78.0% vs. 70.0%). AgentCPM-Explore further reports that online environment instability is a major source of reward noise, limiting its RL gains to only +3.8% over the SFT baseline on GAIA. Our deterministic local environment eliminates such noise, sustaining over 700 stable RL steps with monotonic improvements.

Context length and BrowseComp. BrowseComp requires exceptionally deep browsing chains, often exceeding 20 pages per query. For a 4B model, this frequently exhausts the 128K context window, causing performance degradation (20.3%/28.4% without memory, Table 9). A memory mechanism that summarizes prior tool interactions at 64K mitigates this, improving results to 27.5%/32.5%. This gap highlights long-context utilization as a key limitation of small-scale agents, and we report both configurations for transparency.

5.3 Analysis and Ablations

Local Environment vs. Live Internet.

Over the full RL run, our agents issued 45.8M search queries and 27.4M browse requests—totaling 73.2M tool calls. As shown in Table 3, fulfilling this volume through commercial search engines and browser proxies would cost $59K–$243K, whereas our fully local pipeline incurs zero marginal cost. Beyond the cost saving, the 10–46×\times latency advantage directly translates to higher rollout throughput, making our local ecosystem a prerequisite—not merely an optimization—for scalable on-policy agentic RL.

Effect of Our Synthetic Data.

Our synthesis pipeline produces data diverse enough to cover real-world search patterns and support strong generalization (Table 4): combining our synthetic data with multi-hop data achieves 66.8% on GAIA and 71.0% on Xbench. Removing our synthetic data drops performance to 58.7%/66.3%, confirming that it covers diverse search patterns.

Training Data GAIA Xbench
Multi-hop only 58.7% 66.3%
Ours + multi-hop 66.8% 71.0%

On-Policy vs. Off-Policy Training.

We compare a strictly on-policy algorithm, where each rollout batch is consumed in a single update and then discarded, with a more off-policy algorithm, where each rollout batch is split into multiple mini-batches (e.g., 256 samples into 4 mini-batches) and used for several successive updates. As shown in Figure 3, the off-policy variant gains reward much earlier but eventually declines, whereas on-policy training continues to improve more steadily throughout training. Figure 3 shows that on-policy training achieves higher GAIA validation accuracy (68.9%) than off-policy training (66.8%).

These results suggest that long-horizon Agentic RL is particularly sensitive to off-policy updates. We hypothesize that multiple updates on the same rollout batch introduce policy lag, leading to increasing mismatch between the sampled trajectories and the current policy. In long-horizon search tasks, such mismatch can accumulate along the trajectory, harming optimization stability and ultimately limiting the achievable performance ceiling.

Effectiveness of Multi-Stage Training.

Single-stage RL saturates once the model exhausts tasks at its current difficulty level; deliberate difficulty escalation is the key to continued improvement. Figure 4 shows the learning curves of our two-stage strategy. In Stage 1, the model reaches a plateau at 64.7% GAIA accuracy. After transitioning to Stage 2 with adjusted data distribution and targeted complexity, training continues to improve, reaching 68.3% (+3.6%). This indicates that the second stage helps sustain learning beyond the saturation point of the first, enabled by our unlimited synthetic data pool.

Contribution of RL over SFT.

The SFT stage uses trajectories generated by Tongyi DeepResearch as the teacher model (Appendix B). As shown in Table 9, SFT alone yields 55.6% on GAIA—still 15.3 points below the teacher’s own 70.9%. The RL stage not only closes this gap but surpasses it, reaching 71.3% (+15.7 over SFT), with consistent gains across all eight benchmarks. This indicates that the primary performance driver is the RL training framework rather than teacher distillation.

6 Conclusions

In this paper, we presented LiteResearcher, an agentic RL training framework that resolves the critical bottlenecks of data diversity and environment stability by constructing an isolated virtual world. Crucially, our work yields three key insights for the future of deep research agents. First, we demonstrate that Agentic RL can drive sustained capability improvement. The training saturation observed in prior works is due to reliance on high-variance live environments or a narrow local corpus, rather than a limitation of the RL paradigm itself. Second, we reveal that a simple but scalable synthetic data pipeline, driven by the continuous expansion of real-world information sources, is significantly more effective than over-engineered, handcrafted reasoning structures. Finally, trained entirely locally at zero marginal cost, our compact LiteResearcher-4B achieves 71.3% on GAIA and 78.0% on Xbench-DS. By matching or exceeding commercial models, our results suggest that scalable RL training, beyond model scale alone, is a critical enabler for strong deep research capabilities. The entire training framework, including data synthesis pipelines, local environment infrastructure, and RL training code, will be open-sourced to facilitate future research.

Appendix A Synthetic Data

A.1 Extract Information and Compose QA Prompt

This prompt converts a raw webpage into factual question–answer pairs. We use it to produce single-hop QA items with short, verifiable answers.

A.2 Rubric filter Prompt

This prompt checks whether a QA pair is self-contained and objectively answerable. We use it to filter out vague, open-ended, or non-verifiable items before training.

A.3 Multi-hop QA Synthesis

In addition to the single-hop QA extraction pipeline described in Section 4.1, we employ a separate backward graph-based multi-hop QA synthesis method. The core idea is to first build a knowledge graph grounded in real web evidence, then sample a connected subgraph, and finally generate a question backward from the graph structure so that answering it naturally requires multi-hop reasoning along the graph’s edges. The full pipeline is summarized in Table 5.

A.4 Corpus Evolution

As described in Section 4.1, our corpus grows iteratively: for each validated QA pair, we use the question as a search query to fetch related webpages from the open internet, which are then added to the local corpus. Starting from an initial corpus of ∼\sim10M webpages (Wikipedia and curated seed sources), we expand the corpus by ∼\sim22M additional real web pages over two iterations, reaching a total of ∼\sim32M webpages. The expansion requires ∼\sim220K Serper API calls (each returning ∼\sim100 results), costing only ∼\sim$220—a one-time investment that is negligible compared to the $59K–$243K that would be required if online APIs were used during RL training (Table 3). Table 6 summarizes the corpus statistics at each stage.

Each fetched webpage undergoes deduplication (URL-level and content-hash), HTML-to-Markdown conversion, and minimum length filtering (>>1000 characters). The crawled pages are simultaneously indexed into the local search engine (Milvus) and stored in PostgreSQL for the local browse tool, ensuring that every new page is immediately available for both RL rollouts and subsequent QA synthesis iterations. Figure 5 shows the domain category distribution of the final enriched corpus.

Appendix B SFT Details

B.1 Data Composition

The SFT dataset consists of 68,231 high-quality search trajectories from three categories (Table 7): our co-constructed synthesis pipeline contributes the majority (52.8%), supplemented by multi-hop QA data (7.1%) and trajectories distilled from open-source QA pairs (40.2%). All trajectories are generated by running Tongyi DeepResearch (Team et al., 2025c) as the teacher model on each QA pair with online search tools; we use only the QA pairs from open-source datasets, not their original trajectories.

B.2 Trajectory Processing

Raw trajectories from the teacher model undergo a two-stage processing pipeline (Table 8): seven filtering rules remove low-quality trajectories, and four cleaning steps standardize the surviving data.

Figure 6 shows the distribution of the final 68K trajectories after processing: the mean token length is 12.4K with a long tail extending to ∼\sim45K, and the mean number of interaction turns is 8.7, concentrated around 5–8 turns. The long tail motivates our choice of 64K max sequence length to cover 100% of samples.

B.3 Training and Baseline Performance

We initialize from Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 and perform full-parameter SFT using LLaMA-Factory. All trajectories are formatted using the Qwen3 thinking template with enable_thinking=true. Training uses a maximum sequence length of 64K tokens, a learning rate of 2×10−52\times 10^{-5} with cosine scheduling and 10% warmup, and runs for 1 epoch on 8×\timesH100 GPUs with DeepSpeed ZeRO-2, Flash Attention 2, and Liger Kernel optimizations. The effective batch size is 2×8×8=1282\times 8\times 8=128.

Table 9 shows the performance progression. SFT provides a strong initialization for RL, but leaves substantial room for improvement—particularly on benchmarks requiring complex multi-step reasoning.

Appendix C RL Details

C.1 Data Mixture

Table 10 summarizes the data composition used in each RL stage. Stage 1 uses a simple two-source mixture dominated by direct QA, while Stage 2 diversifies the distribution with wiki-sourced queries, multi-hop subgraph reasoning, and science-domain data to push beyond the Stage 1 plateau. All queries undergo difficulty-aware filtering (pass@8, 1≤c≤71\leq c\leq 7) before being fed to training.

C.2 Reward Function

During RL training, each rollout receives a binary reward based on the correctness of the agent’s final answer. The agent is required to produce its answer within <answer>...</answer> tags. We use Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct as the reward judge for LLM-based semantic judgment.

C.3 RL Training Configuration

Table 11 summarizes the full hyperparameter configuration for our RL training pipeline. We use SGLang as the rollout (inference) engine and FSDP as the training engine.

C.4 Trajectory Behavior During RL

After SFT, the model acquires the basic search workflow and achieves a clear performance gain over the base model. However, we observe that among the incorrectly answered queries, a dominant failure mode is repetitive action loops—the model repeatedly issues the same search query or revisits the same URL without making progress, consuming the token budget on redundant interactions rather than exploring alternative strategies. These repetitive trajectories inflate both the response length and the number of turns without contributing useful information.

Figure 7 tracks four metrics during RL training that jointly show how the model eliminates this failure mode while improving task performance.

The mean reward steadily increases from ∼\sim0.42 to ∼\sim0.70 over 420 steps (Figure 7a), confirming that the agent solves progressively more queries correctly. The remaining three metrics reveal the mechanism behind this improvement: as RL suppresses the repetitive-action loops, the mean response length drops from ∼\sim18K to ∼\sim12K tokens (Figure 7b), the mean number of interaction turns decreases from ∼\sim30 to ∼\sim24 (Figure 7c), and the length clip ratio—the fraction of trajectories truncated for exceeding the context window—falls from ∼\sim0.28 to ∼\sim0.02 (Figure 7d). All three reductions reflect the same underlying cause: the model learns to stop repeating futile actions, resulting in shorter, more purposeful search trajectories.

Notably, this behavioral correction emerges purely from the outcome-based reward signal and the GRPO clipping mechanism, without any explicit length penalty or repetition penalty in the loss function.

C.5 Training Dynamics

We track several metrics across the full two-stage RL training process. Stage 1 (steps 0–220, temperature 0.7) trains on local-RAG-only data, and Stage 2 (from step 220, temperature 1.0) continues from the Stage 1 checkpoint with the full data mixture.

Training dynamics.

Figure 8 summarizes four key metrics across the full two-stage RL process. Panel (a) shows the GAIA validation accuracy: Stage 1 establishes the initial performance gain over the SFT baseline, and Stage 2 further improves accuracy, reaching a peak of ∼\sim68%. Panel (b) shows the policy entropy; Stage 2 uses a higher sampling temperature, resulting in higher absolute entropy, while entropy decreases steadily in both stages, indicating increasingly confident action selection. Panels (c) and (d) jointly plot the average tool calls and trajectory total tokens. During Stage 1, both metrics drop sharply as the model eliminates redundant action loops. In Stage 2, both increase together, indicating the model performs more search steps and generates longer but more productive trajectories.
